domain: Safety Engineering / Organizational Learning / Competence Retention
topic_summary: Analysis of catastrophe-avoidance competence retention in aviation (stall recovery, CRM) and nuclear (meltdown-avoidance) domains, where decades-long safety records depend on simulator-based training without recurring real catastrophes. The kernel contest examines whether simulation counts as the exercise that keeps competence occupied, or whether only real catastrophe truly tests retention.

key_entities: Airlines and nuclear plant operators (training implementers)
ICATEE (international aviation safety working group post-2009 crashes)
EPRI (nuclear severe accident analysis software developer)
Colgan Air/Air France 447 crashes (triggering events for stall recovery mandate)
Fukushima disaster (triggering event for severe accident simulation)
key_tensions: Simulation fidelity vs. real-world irreplaceability (can drills substitute for actual catastrophe experience)
Competence decay without practice vs. decades-long safety record (does simulation prevent decay or merely mask it)
Jeopardy conditions in simulation vs. non-jeopardy line operations (assessment environment vs. operational reality)
Epistemological validation gap (cannot test adequacy without allowing catastrophe)
key_mechanisms: Recurrent simulator training cycles (FAA mandate: all pilots by March 2020; nuclear post-Fukushima)
Competence decay measurement (55% deficiency in 3+ skills at 18 months without practice)
Line audits under non-jeopardy conditions (CRM behavior observation in actual operations)
key_absences: Empirical data on optimal refresher intervals (currencies vs. proficiencies)
Direct comparison of simulation-trained vs. real-catastrophe-experienced operators (ethically impossible)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Catastrophe-avoidance competence must be continuously exercised to remain occupied; the question is what counts as valid exercise
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Regulatory bodies (FAA, NRC) ground legitimacy in safety record and simulation fidelity standards; operators ground legitimacy in demonstrated performance under assessment

readings.commitment: Simulation counts as valid exercise that keeps competence occupied; drills are proxy-catastrophe
readings.authority_grounding: Regulatory mandate + safety record (decades without recurring catastrophe) + transfer-of-training research showing simulation improves performance
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence retention validated through simulation metrics; safety record proves adequacy; regulatory compliance sufficient

readings.commitment: Only real catastrophe truly exercises competence; simulation is insufficient substitute
readings.authority_grounding: Phenomenological irreplaceability (G-forces, turbulence, psychological pressure) + competence decay evidence (55% deficiency at 18 months) + pilot testimony seeking muscle memory refreshers
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence retention remains untested; safety record reflects luck or system redundancy rather than proven adequacy; simulation masks decay

readings.commitment: Simulation is necessary but not sufficient; competence retention requires continuous drill cycles, not one-time validation
readings.authority_grounding: Competence decay research + recurrent training mandates + line audit findings (jeopardy vs. non-jeopardy performance gap)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence retention is process-dependent, not state-validated; safety record proves continuous exercise works, not that simulation equals catastrophe

axiom_contradictions.basis: No single framework can hold both 'simulation is adequate validation' and 'only real catastrophe validates' — one requires accepting simulation fidelity as sufficient, the other requires rejecting it as categorically insufficient regardless of fidelity

omegas.description: The D5 break tests whether the reading distinction collapses. Evidence suggests PARTIAL collapse: simulation demonstrably works (decades-long safety record) but only under continuous refresh cycles. The distinction between 'proxy-catastrophe' and 'real-catastrophe-only' does not fully collapse because competence decay evidence shows simulation alone is insufficient, yet the safety record shows continuous simulation IS sufficient. The paradox is resolved by continuous_refresh_hybrid: simulation works as ongoing process, not as one-time validation equivalent to catastrophe.
omegas.source: Kernel contest specification + competence decay evidence + safety record data

omegas.description: Objective data on optimal refresher intervals is hardly available. Current mandates focus on currencies (time-based) rather than proficiencies (performance-based). This gap means the continuous_refresh_hybrid reading cannot specify the minimum viable refresh frequency—only that some continuous cycle is necessary.
omegas.source: Absence inventory (§1.1) + research context on currency vs. proficiency

omegas.description: Line audits under non-jeopardy conditions provide the most useful data on operational competence, but coverage and frequency are not specified in the research context. If line audits are rare, the jeopardy_condition_gap may be larger than the safety record suggests.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + jeopardy condition research

omegas.description: Nuclear severe accident simulation was introduced POST-Fukushima. The counterfactual (would pre-Fukushima simulation have prevented the disaster) is unknowable, but it suggests the real_catastrophe_only reading may have empirical support: the catastrophe revealed inadequacy that simulation had not addressed.
omegas.source: Research context on Fukushima triggering severe accident simulation + epistemological validation gap

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition into three readings captures the structural contest. The D5 collapse test is addressed in omega_d5_collapse_test: partial collapse, resolved by continuous_refresh_hybrid reading.
